author: Grace Chen
title: Gyeonggi-do COVID-19 Response & Infectious Disease System
text:
Gyeonggi-do Bolsters Infectious Disease Response with Expanded Investigator Network & Proactive Prevention Measures Gyeonggi Province is significantly enhancing its public health infrastructure, investing in a larger team of epidemiological investigators and implementing comprehensive strategies to combat both emerging and established infectious diseases. These efforts, announced on June 3rd, aim to strengthen surveillance, accelerate response times, and protect vulnerable populations.
Rapid Response to Emerging threats Recognizing the critical need for preparedness,Gyeonggi-do has established a robust system for responding to high-threat infectious diseases like Ebola and Middle East Respiratory syndrome (MERS). This includes a 24-hour emergency service, dedicated personnel, and a streamlined emergency contact network. “The ability to secure and quarantine beds within an hour of receiving a report is a game-changer,” stated a senior provincial health official.The province responded to 289 cases of overseas inflow quarantine for first-class infectious diseases in 2024 and an additional 142 cases through June 2025, demonstrating the system’s immediate impact.
Did You Know? Gyeonggi-do’s rapid response system includes drills and simulations to ensure personnel are prepared for real-world scenarios involving high-threat infectious diseases. These exercises test dialogue protocols, quarantine procedures, and treatment strategies. Expanding the Epidemiological Workforce The province dramatically increased its capacity for infectious disease control beginning in 2020, coinciding with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.This expansion was further supported by revisions to the infectious disease prevention law in March of the same year,enabling municipalities to appoint their own epidemiological investigation officers. As of June 2024, Gyeonggi-do boasts 109 epidemiological investigators across its 9 cities and 100 counties, all equipped with specialized expertise. Beyond simply increasing numbers, the province has prioritized skill progress, launching the Gyeonggi-do Epidemiologist Infectious Disease conference (held twice in 2023 and 2024) and establishing the “Epidemiological investigator Academy” and “Strategic Planning and Training” programs to enhance practical response capabilities.
Key Initiative: The Epidemiological Investigator Academy provides advanced training in data analysis, outbreak investigation techniques, and risk communication, ensuring a highly skilled workforce capable of effectively managing infectious disease outbreaks. Tackling Endemic Diseases: malaria & Tuberculosis Gyeonggi-do is also intensifying its focus on controlling endemic infectious diseases. A proactive approach to malaria prevention, initiated in 2023, includes in-depth epidemiological investigations and early warning systems for cluster cases. These measures have yielded positive results, with the number of malaria cases decreasing by 9.4% from 434 in 2023 to 393 in 2024, and further declining to 96 cases by June 2024 – a 17% reduction compared to the same period last year. Resources are being strategically allocated to high-risk areas like Paju, Gimpo, and Goyang, with customized consulting services offered to minimize outbreaks.
malaria Prevention Spotlight: Gyeonggi-do utilizes mosquito surveillance and targeted insecticide spraying in high-risk areas to control mosquito populations and reduce the risk of malaria transmission. Community education programs also play a vital role in promoting personal protective measures. Similarly, the province is making notable strides in tuberculosis control.Through preemptive screenings,especially in high-density populations and in collaboration with private medical institutions,tuberculosis cases have been reduced by 25.8% – from 5,491 in 2020 to 4,073 in 2024. The “Visiting Tuberculosis Screening Project” has examined 14,022 vulnerable individuals (including the elderly and homeless) over the past five years, leading to the early treatment of 99 identified cases. Looking ahead to 2027, Gyeonggi-do plans to further tighten screening protocols for vulnerable groups, aiming for fewer than 20 tuberculosis cases per 100,000 population. .
Tuberculosis control Innovation: The “Visiting Tuberculosis Screening Project” employs mobile screening units to reach vulnerable populations, providing convenient access to testing and early diagnosis. This proactive approach is crucial in preventing the spread of tuberculosis within these communities. Strengthening Vaccination Programs Gyeonggi-do is committed to expanding and refining its national vaccination programs. The provincial budget allocated to vaccination initiatives has increased by approximately 17% – from ₩1.772 trillion in 2019 to ₩206.5 billion currently – demonstrating a considerable investment in preventative healthcare. The province also successfully advocated for improvements to the national vaccination system, specifically regarding the collection of contact information to improve inoculation rates among vulnerable groups. This year,a key focus is on protecting seniors,with a new initiative providing influenza vaccination for workers in nursing hospitals and community care facilities,targeting 51,702 individuals across 3,944 facilities with a budget of approximately ₩930 million.
Vaccination Program Highlight: Gyeonggi-do’s influenza vaccination program for senior care workers not only protects these essential personnel but also helps to prevent outbreaks within vulnerable populations residing in nursing homes and community care facilities. These comprehensive efforts underscore Gyeonggi-do’s dedication to safeguarding public health and building a resilient community prepared to face the challenges of infectious diseases.
